It follows from their disavowal of his worship that they also disavow the worshipped One, because worship is directed toward Him, and this is not a valid point.

For the intent is: his disavowal of their gods, and his informing them that they are disavowed from the God, the Exalted.

So the intended object is the worshipped One, not the act of worship.

It was also said: they intended to oppose him ﷺ out of envy and disdain for his followers.

So they did not worship his Worshipped One out of hatred for the Worshipped One's essence, but out of hatred for following him ﷺ and eagerness to oppose him in worship.

On this view, in the wondrous arrangement and the sublime meaning, only the word "mā" is appropriate, because of its generality and its matching the purpose contained in the verse.

A fourth aspect was also mentioned, namely: intending a parallelism in the eloquence and fluency of the speech, like His saying: ﴿They forgot God, so He caused them to forget themselves﴾ and ﴿Whoever aggresses against you, then aggress against him in the same way﴾. and similar examples.

Its parallel is His saying ﴿so marry what is good for you of women﴾. Since the intended meaning was the attribute, and the motivating cause for the command to marry, and its aim, namely goodness, so that a woman described by it is married, He used "mā" rather than "man." Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 109, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

A ninth benefit: in His saying, ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾, there is a meaning beyond the earlier negation, for it indicates the exclusivity of each party to its own religion and its own object of worship. This is understood from the negation itself, so what benefit does the stated division add?

A tenth benefit: the mention of them and their object of worship is placed first in this division and exclusivity, while the mention of His own affair and action is placed first at the beginning of the surah.

An eleventh benefit: this surah contains two kinds of statements.
The first: His disavowal of their object of worship, and their disavowal of His object of worship; this is constant and perpetual.
The second: His statement that his religion is for him and their religion is for them.
So is this a disengagement and a silence about them, such that it is subject to abrogation (naskh) by the sword, or a restriction to some of the disbelievers? Or is the verse still in its generality and its ruling, neither abrogated nor restricted?

These are ten questions in this surah. We have already mentioned one of them, namely the use of ﴿مَا﴾ (ma) in place of ﴿مَنْ﴾ (man).

Let us now mention the nine remaining questions, seeking help from God's bounty, asking Him for strength and power, and disclaiming error before Him. Whatever is correct is from Him alone, without partner, and whatever is in error is from us and from Satan, and God and His Messenger are free of it.

As for the second question, which concerns the benefit of repeating the verbs: several views have been expressed about it.

The first: His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is a negation of the present and the future.
His saying ﴿And you are not worshippers of what I worship﴾ is its counterpart, meaning you will not do that.
His saying ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ means that this never came from me before the revelation was sent down. For this reason, He used the past tense for their worship, saying ﴿what you have worshipped﴾, as if He said: I never worshipped what you have worshipped.
His saying ﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ is its counterpart, meaning you never in the past worshipped what I have always worshipped.
On this view there is no repetition at all. The verses have covered all the divisions of negation, past, present and future, regarding His worship and their worship, in the most concise, most precise and clearest wording. This, God willing, is the best of what has been said about it, so let us confine ourselves to it and not go beyond it to others.
For the views that have been expressed in their places, you should consult them.

As for the third question, which concerns the repetition of the verbs, using the future form when He speaks of Himself and the past form when He speaks of them:
In this there is a secret, namely an indication and allusion to God's protection of His Prophet from deviation and swerving from the worship of his Lord, and from substituting another for Him, and that his Lord, the true object of worship, is one in the present and in the outcome, constantly, not accepting another in His place, nor desiring a change from Him. This is unlike the disbelievers, who worship their own desires and follow their own appetites and aims in religion. They are on the verge of worshipping one object today and another tomorrow. So He said: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, meaning now, and ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, meaning also now.
Then He said: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾, meaning: nor, in the future, will worship proceed from me to what you have worshipped, O disbelievers. Here ﴿مَا﴾ resembles the scent of a conditional, so the verb after it came in the past form, though it is future in meaning, as this occurs after the conditional particle, as if he were saying: whatever you have worshipped of anything, I do not worship it.
If it is said: how can there be a conditional in it, when the verb has operated on it, and it has no answer, since it is a relative? How far is the conditional from it?
We reply: we did not say that it is itself a conditional, but there is in it a scent of it, and a trace of its meaning, because it falls upon an unspecified object, and because of its vagueness regarding the objects of worship and its generality. When you taste the meaning of this statement, you will find the meaning of the conditional manifest on its surface. If you say to a man, one who opposes you in everything he does: I do not do what you do. Do you not see the meaning of the conditional established in your speech and intention, and that the essence of this statement is: whatever thing you do, I do not do it?
Consider this from the example of God's saying: ﴿They said: How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ How do you find the sense of the conditional in it, so that the verb after ﴿مَنْ﴾ came in the past form while the meaning is future, and the sense is: how can we speak to one who is, in the cradle, a child? This is the meaning which some of the exegetes and grammarians circled around when they said that ﴿كان﴾ (kana) means ﴿يكون﴾ (yakun). But they did not approach it from its proper gate; rather they left it stripped of estimation and interpretation, and the understanding of others strayed from this because of its subtlety and fineness.
So they said: ﴿كان﴾ is superfluous (zā'ida).
The correct view is what I have told you, so take it freely: you gain its benefit and I bear its burden. Regarding ﴿مَنْ﴾ in the verse, the verb has operated on it and it has no answer, and the conditional sense subsists in it; likewise in His saying: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾. All this is understood from the speech of the leading grammarians such as al-Zajjaj and others.
When this is established, the wisdom for which the verb came in the past form in His saying ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ is confirmed, unlike His saying ﴿Nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾, because ﴿مَا﴾ there is far from the meaning of the conditional. This is a reminder from God of the protection of His Prophet from having any object of worship other than Him, and from shifting among objects of worship as the disbelievers shift.

As for the fourth question: in regard to them, the negation came only with the active participle, while in regard to Himself it came sometimes with the verb and sometimes with the active participle.
This, God knows best, is for a wondrous wisdom, namely that the greatest purpose is His disavowal of their objects of worship in every respect and at every time. So He first used the verbal form, which indicates occurrence and renewal, then in this same negation He used the form of the active participle in the second instance: this is not my attribute nor my condition. As if He said: worship other than God does not become an act of mine nor a description of me. Thus He gave two negations for two negated matters, both intended by the negation. As for them, He used only the noun that indicates attribute and permanence, not the verb. That is, the established, binding attribute belonging to God is negated for you; this attribute is not established for you, but is established for one who singled out God alone for worship and did not associate anyone with Him in it. And since you have worshipped other than Him, you are not among His worshippers. Even if they worship Him at some times, the polytheist worships God and worships others along with Him, as the People of the Cave said: ﴿And when you withdrew from them and what they worship except God﴾, meaning you withdrew from their objects of worship, except God, for you did not withdraw from Him. Likewise the polytheists said of their objects of worship: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us near to God in nearness﴾. So they used to worship other than Him along with Him, and the act was not negated of them since it occurred from them, but the attribute was negated, because one who worships other than God does not remain steadfast in the worship of God, nor is he described by it.
Reflect on this wondrous point, and see how you find folded within it that one is not described as a worshipper of God, nor as one who is upright in His worship, except one who has devoted himself to Him entirely and dedicated himself to Him with complete devotion, turning to no one else and associating no one with Him in His worship. And if he worships Him and associates another with Him, he is neither a worshipper of God nor a servant of His.
This is among the secrets of this great and majestic surah, which is one of the two surahs of sincere devotion (al-Ikhlas), which equals one quarter of the Qur'an, as has come in some of the hadith collections. This is not understood by everyone, and no one grasps it except one whom God has granted understanding from Himself. To Him be praise and grace.

As for the fifth question: the negation in this surah came with the particle ﴿لا﴾ (la) rather than ﴿لن﴾ (lan). This is because it has been previously established closely that negation with ﴿لا﴾ is stronger than with ﴿لن﴾, and that it indicates the perpetuity and length of the negation more than ﴿لن﴾ does, and that because of the lengthening and extension in its sound, the negation with it is prolonged and intensified. This is the opposite of what the Jahmiyya and the Mu'tazila understood, namely that ﴿لن﴾ negates only the future and does not negate a continuing present negation extending into the future. This has been established previously in a manner you will hardly find outside this commentary. So the use of ﴿لا﴾ is definite here. And God knows best.

As for the sixth question: the surah's inclusion of pure negation. This is the distinctive feature of this great surah, for it is the surah of disavowal of polytheism, as has come in its description: that it is a disavowal of polytheism. Its greatest purpose is the disavowal that is sought. This is so even though it explicitly contains affirmation.
His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is pure disavowal, and ﴿nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ is an affirmation that He has an object of worship whom He alone is worshipped, and you are free of His worship. Thus it contains both negation and affirmation, and it corresponds to the saying of Abraham, the leader of the upright monotheists: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who originated me﴾, and it corresponds to the saying of the monotheist group: ﴿And when you withdrew from them and what they worship except God﴾. Thus it comprises the reality of "there is no god but God." For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pair it with the surah ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ in the Fajr sunna and the Maghrib sunna.
For these two surahs are the surahs of sincere devotion, and they comprise both kinds of monotheism, without which a servant has no salvation and no success: the monotheism of knowledge and belief, which includes glorifying God above what is not fitting for Him of polytheism, disbelief, offspring and parentage, and that He is the One, the Eternal Refuge, who has not begotten, so that He would have an offspring, and has not been begotten, so that He would have a source, and there is none comparable to Him, so that He would have an equal. Together with this, He is the Self-Sufficient Lord in whom all attributes of perfection are gathered.
Thus the surah includes the affirmation of what befits His majesty of the attributes of perfection, and the negation of what does not befit Him of partners, whether origin, offspring, or equal. This is the monotheism of knowledge and belief.
The second is the monotheism of intention and will, which is that none is worshipped but Him, so that no one is associated with Him in worship, but He alone is the object of worship.
The surah ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ comprises this monotheism.
Thus the two surahs embrace both kinds of monotheism and are sincere to it. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to open the day with them in the Fajr sunna and close it with them in the Maghrib sunna.
It is related in the Sunan that "he used to pray the witr with them."
So they are the conclusion of the night's worship just as they were the conclusion of the day's worship.
From here comes the answer to the seventh question, namely: the placement of His disavowal of their object of worship first, then He followed it with their disavowal of His object of worship. Reflect on it.

As for the eighth question, namely: why the address here is with ﴿O you disbelievers﴾ rather than "O you who have disbelieved." I say, God knows best, that the intention is to indicate that whoever has disbelief as a fixed, binding attribute that never leaves him, is worthy that God disavow him, and that he too be free of God. Thus the sincere monotheist is worthy to disavow him. So it was in the context of disavowal, which is the utmost distance and separation, based on the reality of his state, which is the utmost of disbelief, namely established and binding disbelief, in the utmost appropriateness. As if He says: just as disbelief is binding on you, established, from which you do not move, so my separation from you and my disavowal of you is established for me always and forever. For this reason He used in it the negation that indicates continuity, in opposition to the established, continuous disbelief. And this is clear.

As for the ninth question, namely: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾, and does this add a meaning beyond what came before?
It is said: in this there is wisdom, God knows best: the first negation conveyed disavowal, and that it is not conceivable from Him, nor fitting for Him, that He should worship their objects of worship, and that they too would not be worshippers of His object of worship. The end of the surah conveyed the affirmation of what the negation included on their side of polytheism and disbelief, which is their portion, their share and their lot. This is like the case of two men who divide a piece of land between them, and one says to the other: do not enter my boundary, and I will not enter yours; your land is yours, and mine is mine.
Thus the verse includes that this disavowal required that we divide our allotment between us: monotheism and faith fell to us, and this is our share and division, which we are exclusively entitled to, and do not share with you in it. And polytheism with God and disbelief in Him fell to you, and this is your share and division, which you are exclusively entitled to, and we do not share with you in it. Blessed is He who gives life to the hearts of whomever He wills of His servants by understanding His speech.
These meanings and their like, when they are manifested to hearts walking in their finery, they captivate hearts and take hold of their very core. And whoever does not find life in his heart, these are a bride led to a blind, paralyzed man. So praise be to God for His gifts, which have no end, and we ask Him to complete His favour.

As for the tenth question, namely: the placement of their share and portion before His share and portion. At the beginning of the surah He placed what is exclusive to Him before what is exclusive to them.
This is one of the secrets of speech and a wondrous address that none grasps except the masters of eloquence and its champions. The surah required the disavowal and the division of the two religions, monotheism and polytheism, between Him and them, with each content with its share, and the one in the right being the owner of the division. He has displayed the two portions and distinguished the two divisions, and He knows that they are content with their lowly share, than which none is baser or meaner, while He has seized the nobler share and the greater portion. It is like the case of a man who divides with another poison and cure: he consents to the division of poison, and the other says to him: do not share in my portion, and I will not share in yours; your portion is yours, and mine is mine.
So placing the mention of His share here is better and more eloquent, as if He says: this is your share, which you preferred to be put first, and claimed to be the nobler of the two divisions and more worthy of precedence. So in placing the mention of His share first there is mockery of them, and a proclamation of the badness of their choice and the ugliness of what they accepted for themselves, which is not found in placing first the mention of one's own share. The judge in this is taste, and the discerning person is satisfied with the slightest indication, while the dull of understanding is not helped by abundant explanation.
A second aspect: the purpose of the surah is the Prophet's (ﷺ) disavowal of their religion and their object of worship. This is its core and its aim. The mention of their disavowal of his religion and object of worship came as a secondary purpose, completing his disavowal and confirming it. So since the intention was his disavowal of their religion, He began with it at the beginning of the surah.
Then came His saying ﴿For you is your religion﴾ corresponding to this meaning, that is: I do not share with you in your religion, nor do I agree with you about it, but it is a false religion exclusive to you, and I do not share it with you ever. Thus the end of the surah corresponds to its beginning. Reflect on it.

As for the eleventh question, namely: is this statement that for them is their religion and for Him is His religion an acknowledgement, so that it would be abrogated, or is there no abrogation or restriction in the verse?
This is a noble question, among the most important of the questions mentioned. Many have erred regarding this surah and thought it abrogated by the verse of the sword, believing that this verse required the affirmation of them in their religion. Others thought it restricted to those who are allowed to remain in their religion, namely the People of the Book. Both views are pure error. There is no abrogation in the surah and no restriction; rather it is decisive (muhkam), its generality is an established text, and it is among the surahs in which abrogation cannot enter its content, for the rulings of monotheism on which the call of the messengers agreed cannot admit abrogation. This surah has purified monotheism, and for this reason it is called the surah of sincere devotion, as has preceded.
The source of the error: they thought the verse required their being left in their religion, then saw that this leave was removed by the sword, so they said: it is abrogated.
Another group said: it was removed from some disbelievers, namely those who have no scripture. So they said: this is restricted to the People of the Book.
Far be it from God that the verse required affirmation of them or acknowledgement of their religion ever. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the very beginning and at its most intense was always more severe in denouncing them, reproaching their religion, condemning it and forbidding it, threatening and warning them at all times and in every gathering. They asked him to cease mentioning their gods and reproaching their religion, and to leave them to their affair, but he refused except to persist in denouncing them and reproaching their religion. So how can it be said that the verse required his affirmation of them? Far be it from God, this false claim. The verse only required his pure disavowal, as has preceded, and that what you are upon of religion we do not agree with you upon ever, for it is a false religion, exclusive to you, we do not share it with you, nor do you share with us our true religion.
This is the utmost of disavowal and of distancing oneself from agreeing with them in their religion. Where then is the acknowledgement, so that abrogation or restriction would be called for?
Do you think that if they were struggled against with the sword as they were struggled against with proof, it would not be correct to say: ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾? Rather this is a firm, decisive, established verse between believers and disbelievers until God purifies His servants and lands from them.
Likewise the ruling of this disavowal among the followers of God's Messenger (ﷺ), the People of his Sunna, and between the People of innovations who oppose what he brought and call to other than his Sunna: when the successors of the Messenger and his heirs say to them: for you is your religion, and for us is our religion. This does not require their being left in their innovation. Rather they say this to them as a disavowal of them and of their innovation. And together with this they stand ready to refute them and to struggle against them to the extent possible.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 109, verse 6 (part 2 of 2):

This is what Allah, the Mighty, has opened to me by way of these brief words and this stimulating summary, pointing to the greatness of this surah, its sublimity, its purpose, and the wondrous arrangement of its composition. It is without reliance on any tafsir (exegesis), and without tracing these words to sources where they might be found. Rather, it is a drawing-out of what Allah taught and inspired, by His grace and generosity. Allah knows that if I had found these words in a book, I would have attributed them to their author and greatly praised them. It is hoped that Allah, who bestows by His vast grace, whose giving is beyond the measure of created beings, will help me compose a tafsir in this manner and style.

I have written on scattered passages of the Qur'an, as this manner occurred to me, during my stay in Makkah and in Bayt al-Maqdis. And Allah is the One whose completion of His blessing is hoped for.

(Section: Is Disbelief One Religion?)

Those who hold that disbelief is one religion (millah) say: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:120]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshipers of what I worship, nor am I a worshiper of what you have worshiped, nor are you worshipers of what I worship. For you is your religion, and for me is my religion."﴾ [al-Kafirun 109:1–6]

So He made for them one religion, just as He made for the Jews and the Christians one religion.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The people are one category (hayyiz), and I and my companions are one category."

Allah the Exalted divided His creation into disbelievers and believers. These are the happy and those are the wretched. Disbelief, although its branches differ, is comprised of two characteristics:

The first: denying the Messenger in what he reports.

The second: not submitting to his command.

Just as faith returns to two foundations:

The first: obeying the Messenger in what he commands.

The second: affirming what he reports.

Others said: Their sharing in general disbelief does not necessitate their being equal in their religions, for they all share in the Hellfire despite the differences in their degrees of disbelief. Allah's saying ﴿until you follow their religion﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:120] does not indicate that the religion of the Jews is the religion of the Christians. Rather, attributing "religion" to all of them does not require that they share the very same religion. Likewise His saying ﴿For you is your religion, and for me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun 109:6] does not require that they share one religion such that these people adhere to exactly what those people adhere to. Rather, the meaning is: for each of you is his religion and his creed. Allah, glorified is He, mentions truth, guidance, and Islam and makes them one, and He mentions falsehood, misguidance, and disbelief and makes them plural. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am 6:153].

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is the ally of those who believe; He brings them out of darknesses into light. And those who disbelieve – their allies are the taghut (false objects of worship); they bring them out of light into darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:257].

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me. But they divided their affair among themselves into sects; each faction, in what they have, is pleased﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:52–53].

And Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

"The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew a line and said, 'This is the path of Allah.' Then he drew lines to its right and to its left and said, 'These are paths; over each path is a devil calling to it.' Then he recited His saying: ﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way. That He has enjoined upon you, that you may be mindful.﴾"
